title: The Roast

jokes.text: I thought I smelled a publicity man on the premises.
jokes.setup: Norman arrives and greets Artie warmly.
jokes.punchline: Artie's dry greeting implies PR people are detectable by a distinct, unpleasant odor — a worldweary insider's contempt for the flacks.
jokes.explanation: Classic Artie: contemptuous, world-weary, perfectly economical. The joke is entirely in character — only Artie delivers disdain this elegantly. Strong opener that establishes tone.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I thought I smelled a publicity man on the premises.

jokes.text: I remember the night they did Totie Fields. I think I heard every one-legged joke there ever was that night. Oh, Totie, honey, we miss you.
jokes.setup: Artie fondly recalls old Hollywood roasts.
jokes.punchline: The loving nostalgia for one-legged jokes about a deceased comedian — then the tender 'we miss you' — makes the darkness exponentially funnier. He's both celebrating and eulogizing her via her disability.
jokes.explanation: The tonal whiplash between 'every one-legged joke' and the sincere 'we miss you' is the joke. It's vintage Larry Sanders Show — Hollywood's insider culture reducing people to their most exploitable trait, then mourning them. Only Artie, a man of that era, can say this and make it somehow warm. Strong craft.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I remember the night they did Totie Fields. I think I heard every one-legged joke there ever was that night.

jokes.text: Beverly, you know, get her a ticket. / What should I wear? Is it formal? / Oh, my God, girl, if you're going to a roast, I gotta take you shopping, teach you how to dress.
jokes.setup: Artie casually invites Beverly, the receptionist, to Larry's roast as an afterthought.
jokes.punchline: Beverly's naive excitement ('Is it formal?') and the other woman's immediate fashion intervention play as a sweet, small-scale comedy of social worlds colliding — the showbiz royalty event vs. the front-desk staff.
jokes.explanation: Light, functional moment. Beverly's innocent enthusiasm is charming but the joke is fairly thin — the comedy relies on the contrast between worlds but doesn't push it far enough to be memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, my God, girl, if you're going to a roast, I gotta take you shopping, teach you how to dress.

jokes.text: Hank barging in to announce he wants to be 'roast master' — and insisting on the term 'roast mastering.'
jokes.setup: Artie and Norman are having a private professional conversation.
jokes.punchline: Hank interrupts with maximum self-importance to claim the hosting role, insisting on the pompous term 'roast mastering' with complete sincerity. His pedantry about terminology reveals bottomless narcissism.
jokes.explanation: Peak Hank behavior — the insistence on 'roast mastering' as a technical term is a perfect encapsulation of his need to elevate himself through jargon. The joke is entirely in Jeffrey Tambor's delivery and the character's transparent vanity.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I believe technically it's called roast mastering

jokes.text: Oh, Carl Reiner! Come on! That whole stand-up thing is just over. I mean, 'have you noticed this' and 'have you noticed that?' I could do fucking stand-up in my sleep.
jokes.setup: Artie explains Carl Reiner is a 'legendary comedian' who will host.
jokes.punchline: Hank dismisses one of Hollywood's genuine legends with breathtaking condescension, reducing all observational comedy to a verbal tic — then immediately demonstrates he cannot do it.
jokes.explanation: Superb character work. Hank's dismissal of Carl Reiner as passé, then his crude Clinton joke as proof of his own observational genius, is a perfect two-beat comedy of self-delusion. The gap between his self-image and reality is the show's central engine, and this is a textbook example.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Come on! That whole stand-up thing is a... it's just over. I mean, 'have you noticed this,' and 'have you noticed that?'

jokes.text: Hillary Clinton may be Bill Clinton's first lady, but she is not his first lay. Ha ha ha. See? I notice stuff, too. I just don't write it down and go to some moth-eaten nightclub and repeat it.
jokes.setup: Hank claims he could do observational stand-up as well as Carl Reiner.
jokes.punchline: He delivers a hack political sex joke as his proof of genius, then doubles down with smug self-congratulation. The joke is not that the Clinton joke is funny — it's that Hank thinks it is.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's standout moments. The craft is in the layering: the Clinton joke itself is deliberately terrible and hack (a moth-eaten wordplay on 'lay/lady') — which is the whole point. Hank's beaming 'See? I notice stuff, too' is the actual punchline. Then the kicker — denouncing the very format he just attempted — is a perfect three-beat structure. Could only be Hank. Justifies 8.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hillary Clinton may be Bill Clinton's first lady, but she is not his first lay.

jokes.text: I don't think you're built for it, baby. / You don't think that I can handle hecklers? — Hank immediately demands to be heckled to prove himself.
jokes.setup: Artie says Hank can't handle hecklers.
jokes.punchline: Hank's instant, desperate need to prove himself by demanding live heckle practice from his disinterested boss is a perfect comedy of wounded pride.
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for what follows. The comedy is in Hank's wounded dignity demanding immediate vindication from the very person who doubted him. Good character work, but the punchline comes in the next beat.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: See? I notice stuff, too. I just don't write it down and go to some moth-eaten nightclub and repeat it.

jokes.text: Listen, I'm very busy, and I got a sore throat. / Come on! Heckle me! Come on, don't worry, hit me hard.
jokes.setup: Artie tries to beg off heckling Hank.
jokes.punchline: Artie's exhausted excuse ('I got a sore throat') against Hank's desperate pleading creates a beautiful asymmetry — one man with everything to prove, one man who can't be bothered.
jokes.explanation: The 'sore throat' excuse is perfectly mundane against the grandiosity of Hank's ambition. Good cringe setup for the explosion to follow.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Get off the stage, ya fucking moron! I've taken shits more interesting than you are! You're nothin' but Larry Sanders' personal fuck-bitch!

jokes.text: Get off the stage, ya fucking moron! I've taken shits more interesting than you are! You're nothin' but Larry Sanders' personal fuck-bitch! So shut your fucking fat face and get your goddamn bloated ass off the stage, motherfucker!
jokes.setup: Hank asks Artie to heckle him gently. Artie has a sore throat and doesn't want to.
jokes.punchline: Artie unloads a full nuclear heckle with no ramp-up whatsoever, obliterating Hank with brutal specificity and genuine venom — including 'Larry Sanders' personal fuck-bitch,' which is both cruel and precisely accurate.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best moments. The comedy is multi-layered: (1) Artie goes from 'I have a sore throat' to maximum-force heckle with zero transition; (2) the heckle is genuinely devastating and specific — 'Larry Sanders' personal fuck-bitch' is both a roast insult and a character truth about Hank's entire existence on the show; (3) Rip Torn's Artie doing this with full commitment is both terrifying and hilarious. The economy of the setup-to-explosion ratio is masterful. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Good comeback.

jokes.text: Good comeback.
jokes.setup: Hank is visibly destroyed by Artie's heckle. He says 'Oh, Jesus, Artie.'
jokes.punchline: Artie's flat, clinical 'Good comeback' after Hank's devastated response is the perfect period on the joke — dismissing Hank's genuine distress as merely a weak heckle retort.
jokes.explanation: Two words. Perfect. The economy is flawless — Artie weaponizes Hank's wounded 'Oh, Jesus, Artie' by reframing it as a failed heckle retort rather than legitimate human distress. It's contemptuous, precise, and entirely in character. This is Rip Torn's comedy at its most potent. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.line: You mean after his other best friend, Jeffrey Dahmer?

jokes.text: Aw, shut up! Shut up and leave me alone, Phil! I'll come when I'm goddamn ready! / Fucking pig.
jokes.setup: Phil calls for Hank to come to set after the brutal heckle exchange.
jokes.punchline: Hank, freshly humiliated, redirects all his wounded fury at the hapless Phil — then mutters 'fucking pig' as Phil retreats. His dignity reasserts itself by dominating someone even lower in the hierarchy.
jokes.explanation: Good character punctuation. Hank's social hierarchy is a consistent joke engine — he's only dominant over people below him. 'Fucking pig' lands because it's so disproportionate to whatever Phil did.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.line: Jeffrey Dahmer is dead. He's unavailable. I know. That's the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Norman
dialogue.line: What are you, in P.R?

jokes.text: It takes time.
jokes.setup: Hank has just failed catastrophically at demonstrating heckler-handling ability.
jokes.punchline: Artie's philosophical 'It takes time' — delivered presumably to no one, or to himself — treats Hank's total incompetence as merely a matter of practice, which is both generous and damning.
jokes.explanation: Three syllables doing a lot of work. Artie's understatement implies he recognizes a hopeless case but maintains the fiction of improvement. Very Larry Sanders Show in its restraint.

dialogue.speaker: Bill Maher
dialogue.line: I'm as free Saturday night as he is next month.

jokes.text: You mean after his other best friend, Jeffrey Dahmer? / Jeffrey Dahmer is dead. He's unavailable. / I know. That's the joke. / What are you, in P.R.?
jokes.setup: Norman tells Dana he can go on third — after Larry's 'other best friend.'
jokes.punchline: Dana's Jeffrey Dahmer joke is dark and quick, but Norman's literal response ('He's dead. He's unavailable.') followed by Dana's incredulous 'What are you, in P.R.?' is the real comedy — the PR man is so professionally literal he can't process a joke.
jokes.explanation: The three-beat structure is the joke's real strength: dark subversive setup → literal deflation → meta punchline. 'What are you, in P.R.?' is genuinely quotable and lands harder than the Dahmer line itself. The joke about the joke is smarter than the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: all you gotta do is come back with a dick-related insult. That's it.

jokes.text: I thought Larry hated that bit. / No, Larry loves that bit.
jokes.setup: Norman suggests Dana do his telegram bit.
jokes.punchline: Dana's hesitation suggests the real backstory (Larry probably does hate it), and Norman's flat insistence is either a lie or genuine delusion — both readings are funny in the context of Hollywood PR.
jokes.explanation: A functional irony beat. The comedy is in the implied gap between what Dana knows (Larry hates it) and what Norman insists (Larry loves it) — but it's not developed enough to land hard.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: what if the heckler's a woman?

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Well, same thing. You talk about her dick. Makes 'em crazy.

jokes.text: OK, I'll do it, but I'm not gonna go on after Bruno Kirby, because he owes me money and he never brings it up.
jokes.setup: Dana negotiates his appearance at the roast.
jokes.punchline: His deal-breaker isn't creative — it's a petty financial grievance. The specificity of 'he never brings it up' (meaning Dana wants him to feel guilty but Bruno won't) is sharply observed Hollywood pettiness.
jokes.explanation: Economical and specific. 'He never brings it up' is the key detail — Dana wants acknowledgment of the debt, not repayment. The petty psychology is perfectly rendered. Good Hollywood-insider texture.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: I don't come down to your job and knock the dick outta your mouth while you're trying to work.

jokes.text: I've been having kind of a tough time getting him to commit to doing Politically Incorrect next month. / Well, I think I can arrange that. / You're free Saturday night? / I'm as free Saturday night as he is next month.
jokes.setup: Artie invites Bill Maher to the roast.
jokes.punchline: Maher turns the favor-ask into a negotiation in real-time, and Artie matches him perfectly with a mirroring conditional — 'as free Saturday night as he is next month.' The transactional nature of Hollywood friendship laid bare.
jokes.explanation: Sharp showbiz satire — the whole exchange between 'friend' attending a roast and quid pro quo booking is compressed into one elegant transaction. Artie's mirroring line is particularly well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: you can blow me like everyone else on table. At your table.

jokes.text: Come on, Artie, he's a friend, you know? You do things for a friend.
jokes.setup: The Maher booking has just been completed via explicit quid pro quo.
jokes.punchline: Artie's immediate pivot to the language of friendship and loyalty — right after transacting in pure Hollywood currency — is a perfectly ironic button on the scene.
jokes.explanation: A knowing wink at Hollywood friendship mythology. Slight, but it earns its place as a scene button.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Wait a minute. He told me he was going on vacation. Why do they have to lie that way?

jokes.text: Here's the deal. When someone says something to you, all you gotta do is come back with a dick-related insult. That's it.
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to learn heckler comebacks from Phil.
jokes.punchline: Phil's reduction of all roast comedy to 'dick-related insult' is both a pitch-perfect parody of hacky comedy writing and a genuinely useful principle, delivered with complete confidence.
jokes.explanation: Funny inside-comedy-world observation. Phil's taxonomy of roast comedy as 'dick-related insults' is accurate to the genre and slightly self-aware about the episode itself.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Dennis Miller passed. He's very sick. He's in the hospital. Christ! It's like he wants to be caught.

jokes.text: Oh, looks like so-and-so took his dick out of his mouth long enough to speak up.
jokes.setup: Phil gives Hank an example of a dick-related comeback.
jokes.punchline: The example itself is maximally crude and maximally efficient — it's doing exactly what Phil promised and no more.
jokes.explanation: The joke is deliberately hacky — that's the point. It's a meta-comedy about bad roast jokes, but it can't fully transcend its own example. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Very simply, he's the guy we had to take to get Jerry fucking Seinfeld.

jokes.text: Now, by so-and-so, do you mean the person heckling? Yes. I'd better write this down.
jokes.setup: Phil explains the dick comeback template.
jokes.punchline: Hank's need to clarify the basic pronoun reference, then his decision to write it down, is a perfect beat of comedic density — he's both too stupid to understand and too earnest not to try.
jokes.explanation: Hank's sincerity about learning hack comedy is the joke. 'I'd better write this down' is a great character beat — he's treating 'dick-related insults' with the reverence of a master class.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Is mosquito right? Shouldn't it be hung like a bee?

jokes.text: Oh... what if the heckler's a woman? / Well, same thing. You talk about her dick. Makes 'em crazy.
jokes.setup: Hank is worried about the female-heckler exception to the dick-insult rule.
jokes.punchline: Phil's answer — 'talk about her dick' — is aggressively absurdist but delivered with complete tactical confidence. 'Makes 'em crazy' as explanation is the kicker.
jokes.explanation: The absurdist confidence of 'talk about her dick. Makes 'em crazy' is genuinely funny — it's so committed to its own stupid logic. The economy is excellent: maximum comedy per syllable.

dialogue.speaker: Carl Reiner
dialogue.line: For 'the 2,000-year-old man.' We know that was my idea. Your idea was to tell Mel not to do it with a Jewish accent.

jokes.text: This stuff's just good to have in real life.
jokes.setup: Phil has been teaching Hank crude heckler comebacks.
jokes.punchline: Hank's earnest aside that dick-based insults are generally useful life skills is a perfect character beat — his social world is apparently one where this is true.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical character joke. Hank's sincere endorsement of crude insults as life tools tells us everything about his world and his self-image. The line lands because of the sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Get me a damp cloth and a cyanide tablet.

jokes.text: Well, you can blow me like everyone else on table. / At your table.
jokes.setup: Hank attempts to use one of his newly learned heckler comebacks on Phil.
jokes.punchline: He mangles the line — 'on table' instead of 'at your table' — and Phil's flat correction 'At your table' is the punchline. Hank is already failing at the one thing he just learned.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly structured comedy of incompetence. Hank can't even repeat a two-sentence joke correctly immediately after hearing it. Phil's deadpan correction — no emotion, just the correction — is the precise comic beat. Sets up the payoff later when Hank uses both lines at the actual roast.

dialogue.speaker: Dana Carvey (as George Bush)
dialogue.line: Sorry I couldn't make it to your roast, Lar, but I'm bone-fishin' with Barb. Get it? Bone? Barb? Fishin'?

jokes.text: Are you on something? / A little bit.
jokes.setup: Hank has been behaving erratically throughout the scene.
jokes.punchline: Phil's concern and Hank's breezy, unapologetic confirmation that he's on drugs — 'a little bit' — as if this is simply information, is a perfect throwaway.
jokes.explanation: 'A little bit' will recur as a running gag through the episode. The first instance is a good deadpan beat — Hank's casual admission implies this is normal and unremarkable in his world.

dialogue.speaker: Dana Carvey
dialogue.line: Tell Hank to shut the fuck up.

jokes.text: Dennis Miller's a no. He's up in San Francisco. He's doing another fucking HBO special. / Wait a minute. He told me he was going on vacation. / Why do they have to lie that way?
jokes.setup: The team is reviewing RSVPs for the roast.
jokes.punchline: Larry's genuine bewilderment at why celebrities lie about their reasons for declining — 'Why do they have to lie that way?' — is both insider-accurate and a wonderful character note about Larry's naive side.
jokes.explanation: Good showbiz-insider texture. The complaint about polite Hollywood lies resonates as industry satire. Larry's hurt/confused tone makes it more than just cynicism.

dialogue.line: shave my head with a cheese grater... get a barium enema, and check Dom DeLuise's ball sack for lumps.

jokes.text: Mike Ovitz, eating lunch this far away from me, did not look good. You didn't hear it from me, all right? That's a swell story, Stevie, but what's the latest news from Roastville?
jokes.setup: Stevie arrives with Hollywood gossip.
jokes.punchline: Artie's immediate dismissal of a major Hollywood power-shift rumor ('That's a swell story, Stevie') in favor of roast logistics is both funny and reveals Artie's total focus on the job at hand.
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'Roastville' is a funny Artie-ism. The scene efficiently satirizes Hollywood's obsession with proximity to power (Ovitz's table distance as significant data) while Artie cuts through it all.

dialogue.line: tell Hank that Ed said to shut the fuck up.

jokes.text: Dennis Miller passed. He's very sick. He's in the hospital. / Christ! It's like he wants to be caught.
jokes.setup: Stevie covers for Dennis Miller with a new lie (he's in the hospital now).
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'It's like he wants to be caught' treats the escalating lies as a crime being poorly concealed — the comedy is in applying detective logic to Hollywood social cowardice.
jokes.explanation: Sharp and economical. 'It's like he wants to be caught' is a great line — treating social lying as inept criminal behavior. Very much in the show's DNA of applying real-world seriousness to trivial Hollywood behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Dana Carvey
dialogue.line: I just wanna say to Bruno Kirby, you owe me 250 bucks, you little prick. Where is he? Oh, there he is. OK.

jokes.text: I got you Jerry fucking Seinfeld, Larry. / OK, great, that is great. / You really got Seinfeld? Fucking-a.
jokes.setup: The team has been dealing with difficult cancellations.
jokes.punchline: Larry's under-reaction ('OK, great') followed by Artie's genuine excitement reveals the hierarchy — Larry performs cool detachment while Artie drops the pretense and responds authentically. The double 'fucking' as punctuation for celebrity value is also funny.
jokes.explanation: Good character contrast beat. Larry's practiced cool vs. Artie's authentic excitement is a nice reversal of expectations.

dialogue.speaker: Carl Reiner
dialogue.line: The great thing about Larry Sanders is that he never exploited the fact that he was a homosexual. He was gay, he was proud, but he didn't shove it down anybody's throat.

jokes.text: And we also got Kip Addota. Who's he? / Very simply, he's the guy we had to take to get Jerry fucking Seinfeld.
jokes.setup: The team announces a booking.
jokes.punchline: Kip Addota's entire identity is reduced to 'the package deal we had to accept' — a brutally honest description of how show business actually works.
jokes.explanation: Clean and economical Hollywood satire. Reducing a person to their instrumental value ('the guy we had to take') with complete casualness is both accurate and funny.

dialogue.line: Most of it hit you when he tripped over the microphone cord.

jokes.text: What the fuck is this shit? I do not go on last. / Who are you? / Kip Addota. / Of course you are!
jokes.setup: An unknown man storms in complaining about his slot.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'Of course you are!' — implying he has no idea who Kip is but instantly understands everything about him from the complaint — is a perfect put-down that also lands as self-aware about the 'package deal' joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Of course you are!' is the kind of line that gets funnier in retrospect — Artie doesn't know or care who Kip is, but the name itself becomes sufficient explanation. Strong callback payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Carl Reiner
dialogue.line: oh, Christ, I'm not wastin' this on chicks!

jokes.text: Get off the stage, you jerk! / Don't listen to him, everyone. He's just saying that because he's hung like a mosquito. Is mosquito right? Shouldn't it be hung like a bee?
jokes.setup: Kip heckles Hank so he can practice his comeback.
jokes.punchline: Hank's comeback starts strong (dick insult, per training) but then immediately derails into a genuine zoological inquiry about insect anatomy. His inability to maintain comedic commitment by stopping to fact-check the metaphor is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. Hank applies the lesson correctly ('hung like a mosquito') but immediately breaks the comic frame to worry about entomological accuracy. The pivot from insult to genuine inquiry ('Is mosquito right?') is a perfect character-specific joke — only Hank would stop mid-roast to fact-check a metaphor. Great callback structure.

dialogue.line: He's doing his act. He's killing.

jokes.text: Bee. / No, I don't do those anymore.
jokes.setup: Hank is genuinely asking whether 'hung like a bee' is the correct insect.
jokes.punchline: Carl Reiner apparently answers 'Bee' (confirming the anatomy) — then immediately declines the hosting job with 'No, I don't do those anymore.' The total non-sequitur of a legendary comedian providing insect-hung comparative data then declining is perfectly absurd.
jokes.explanation: The economy is extraordinary — 'Bee. / No, I don't do those anymore' does triple work: answers the entomology question, reveals Carl Reiner is present, and declines the roast in one breath. Wonderful compression.

dialogue.speaker: Carl Reiner
dialogue.line: luckily, the camera loves me.

jokes.text: Listen, if you don't host this, I'll have to give it to Hank Kingsley. / I see what your problem is.
jokes.setup: Artie needs Carl Reiner to host the roast.
jokes.punchline: Carl Reiner's 'I see what your problem is' — treating 'Hank Kingsley hosting' as a diagnosable crisis rather than a personnel matter — is the perfect understated response.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's cleaner lines. The compression of 'Hank hosting = obvious crisis' into 'I see what your problem is' is sharp and plays beautifully on everything the audience knows about Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: The bastard cancelled an hour ago.

jokes.text: You've got to! You owe me! / I owe you for what? / For 'The 2,000-Year-Old Man.' We know that was my idea. / Your idea was to tell Mel not to do it with a Jewish accent. / No, my idea was to tell you not to do it with a Jewish accent.
jokes.setup: Artie claims Carl Reiner owes him for an old favor.
jokes.punchline: The 'favor' is that Artie told someone not to do a legendary bit with a Jewish accent — and the bit was famously done entirely in a Jewish accent. Both men remember the bad advice differently. The joke is in the absurdity of claiming credit for universally bad advice.
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely sophisticated joke for comedy insiders. 'The 2,000-Year-Old Man' is one of the most famous comedy albums ever made, entirely defined by Mel Brooks' exaggerated Jewish accent. Artie claiming credit for telling them NOT to do it with a Jewish accent — and then the confusion about who he told — is delightfully absurd. It rewards industry knowledge. Carl's correction makes it funnier, not less. Strong craft, justifies 8.

dialogue.speaker: Kip Addotta
dialogue.line: Like today... we put salt on our asses... and we drove out to that petting zoo.

jokes.text: Look, I'll do it just to get out of this conversation.
jokes.setup: Artie has been twisting Carl Reiner's arm with increasingly absurd rationale.
jokes.punchline: Carl Reiner's capitulation cites conversation-avoidance rather than any of Artie's arguments — the most honest and deflating possible reason to agree to host a Hollywood roast.
jokes.explanation: Clean, economical button on the scene. 'Just to get out of this conversation' is both specific to Artie's conversational persistence and universally relatable. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, then I owe Carrot Top a big apology for last year, don't I? Remember when I said he would suck a cock doing a sack race?

jokes.text: Hank learning he's been bumped for Carl Reiner. 'Aw, that's not fair. That's not fair at all. God damn it! That is not fair.' / Come on, Hank. Be a man. / I'm not going.
jokes.setup: Artie informs Hank that Carl Reiner will host, not him.
jokes.punchline: Hank's repeated, escalating 'that's not fair' — three times, like a child — followed by his petulant 'I'm not going' is a perfect comedy of wounded vanity. 'Be a man' from Artie makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: Classic Tambor/Hank. The repetition of 'not fair' is perfectly calibrated — he says it exactly one time too many to maintain dignity. Artie's 'Be a man' is the ideal straight-man response.

dialogue.line: and Tom Arnold's asshole was booked, so...

jokes.text: Get me a damp cloth and a cyanide tablet.
jokes.setup: Hank is devastated at being bumped as roast master.
jokes.punchline: His theatrical request for a cyanide tablet alongside the very mundane 'damp cloth' is a perfect absurdist pairing — the mundane first-aid alongside the extreme self-pity.
jokes.explanation: Highly quotable and elegantly constructed. The comedy is in the coupling — 'damp cloth AND cyanide tablet,' as if both are equally reasonable requests. The specificity of 'damp cloth' (not 'water,' not 'a towel') makes the absurdity work. Hank's self-pity reaches its logical extreme. One of the episode's best individual lines. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Carl Reiner
dialogue.line: That's the kind of quick wit and jest that keeps you on Larry's couch.

jokes.text: Is he on something? / A little bit.
jokes.setup: Hank requests a cyanide tablet.
jokes.punchline: The 'Is he on something? / A little bit.' exchange recurs — now between Norman and Artie — confirming everyone in the office knows Hank is medicated and no one cares.
jokes.explanation: The running gag is now between two people who aren't Hank, which escalates its comic effect — it's institutional knowledge. 'A little bit' as a three-word running gag is efficiently deployed.

dialogue.speaker: Norm Crosby
dialogue.line: you are absolutely adequate.

jokes.text: I changed my mind about Jon Stewart. I think he should sit as far away from Larry as possible. He can sit in his goddamn car for all I care.
jokes.setup: Earlier it was suggested Stewart should sit near Larry to dispel tension between them.
jokes.punchline: Artie's reversal — from strategic proximity to 'sit in his goddamn car' — suggests the professional situation between Larry and Stewart has deteriorated rapidly, and Artie now wants maximum separation.
jokes.explanation: 'His goddamn car' is a nice escalation from the earlier diplomatic seating strategy. The sudden reversal implies an off-screen development that we're not privy to, which is very Larry Sanders — the show assumes we're insiders.

dialogue.speaker: Norm Crosby
dialogue.line: When I first met Larry Sanders, he was screwing my cousin. And I didn't even know that he knew Harvey.

jokes.text: Oh, you got Dana Carvey. That's terrific. That way there'll be someone there who'll say something nice about Larry.
jokes.setup: Artie reviews the roast lineup.
jokes.punchline: Artie assumes that all other roasters will be cruel and that only Dana, Larry's close friend, will provide any warmth — which is simultaneously a compliment to Dana and a damning indictment of Larry's relationships.
jokes.explanation: Good character insight line. The implication that 'all roasters will roast' makes Dana's assumed loyalty notable — and slightly pathetic for Larry. The economy is solid.

dialogue.speaker: Norm Crosby
dialogue.line: When I first met Larry Sanders, he was screwing my cousin. And I didn't even know that he knew Harvey.

jokes.text: A telegram from George Bush: 'Sorry I couldn't make it to your roast, Lar, but I'm bone-fishin' with Barb. Get it? Bone? Barb? Fishin'?' And he said, 'One more thing. Tell Hank to shut the fuck up.'
jokes.setup: Dana Carvey does his telegram bit at the roast, reading 'from George Bush.'
jokes.punchline: The Bush telegram is a double: the crude bone/Barb/fishing pun (exactly the kind of try-hard joke Bush would make) followed by the kicker 'Tell Hank to shut the fuck up' — which gets a second laugh by bringing the show's internal conflict into the telegram.
jokes.explanation: The George Bush telegram lands on two levels: the character parody (Bush explaining his own joke in parentheses — 'Get it? Bone?') and the callback to Hank's desperation for the spotlight. Bush earnestly explaining a sex pun is perfectly observed Carvey character work.

dialogue.speaker: Norm Crosby
dialogue.line: He's on that new Hollywood agent diet. You can only eat while you're being eaten.

jokes.text: Here's one from Johnny Carson, sent in a sealed envelope. 'Shave my head with a cheese grater, get a barium enema, and check Dom DeLuise's ball sack for lumps. Name 3 things I'd rather do than go to Larry's roast.' P.S., 'Tell Hank that Ed said to shut the fuck up.'
jokes.setup: Dana reads a telegram 'from Johnny Carson.'
jokes.punchline: The Carson telegram goes much darker than Bush — the barium enema / cheese grater / Dom DeLuise formulation is brilliantly specific and escalating, then the 'Name 3 things I'd rather do than go to Larry's roast' Jeopardy-format reveal is the punchline. The 'Ed said' kicker adds another layer.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's single best joke. The structure is near-perfect: three escalating absurd-specific items (the cheese grater, barium enema, and especially 'check Dom DeLuise's ball sack for lumps' — which is specific, visual, and grotesque) leading to a delayed Jeopardy-reveal punchline. It rewards patience — you think the list IS the joke, then discover it's a setup for the format inversion. 'Ed said to shut the fuck up' is a perfect callback kicker. Carson's refusal to attend his own protégé's roast, expressed through maximum specificity, feels exactly right for the show's insider voice. Justifies 8.4.

dialogue.speaker: Norm Crosby
dialogue.line: You just... never seem to be able to get 'em at home.

jokes.text: I just wanna say to Bruno Kirby, you owe me 250 bucks, you little prick. Where is he? Oh, there he is.
jokes.setup: Dana Carvey is wrapping his roast set.
jokes.punchline: Dana publicly calls out Bruno's debt at the roast — escalating the earlier backstage negotiation ('I won't go on after Bruno because he owes me money') to a live public shaming. The addition of 'you little prick' and the searching for Bruno in the crowd is perfect.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff. The earlier negotiation ('I won't go on after Bruno') is paid off by Dana handling it in the most public way possible. 'You little prick' has the affection of real friendship. The moment of scanning the room for Bruno is a great visual beat.

dialogue.speaker: President Clinton
dialogue.line: I'd rather have Al Gore fuck me in the ass.

jokes.text: What a shame. Larry's best friend... and lover, ending it here, where they started, at the Beverly Hilton.
jokes.setup: Carl Reiner introduces the next portion of the evening after Dana.
jokes.punchline: 'Best friend... and lover' — the pause before 'lover' converts a tribute into a jab, and 'ending it here where they started' implies a relationship history at this hotel.
jokes.explanation: The pause before 'and lover' is the classic roast misdirection — set up expectation, subvert with innuendo. Carl Reiner's delivery presumably sells it. Clean structure.

dialogue.speaker: Bruno Kirby
dialogue.line: What the fuck am I doing here? I'm an actor. We do 2 different things. Comedians jerk off. I work.

jokes.text: He was giving Dana a Heimlich maneuver in the restaurant right over there. I remember saying to him, 'Larry, why don't you two guys put some clothes on? The rest of us are eating!'
jokes.setup: Carl Reiner remembers meeting Larry for the first time.
jokes.punchline: The Heimlich maneuver in a restaurant sounds plausible — then 'put some clothes on' retroactively reframes the entire scene into something sexual. The image of emergency medical care performed naked in a restaurant is perfectly absurd.
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection structure. The Heimlich setup is specific enough to be plausible before the clothing reveal recontextualizes everything. The audience pivot ('We're eating here!') is a nice button.

dialogue.speaker: Bruno
dialogue.line: And I don't owe you $250, pal. You owe me $250.

jokes.text: The great thing about Larry Sanders is that he never exploited the fact that he was a homosexual. He was gay, he was proud, but he didn't shove it down anybody's throat.
jokes.setup: Carl Reiner praises Larry's restraint about his alleged homosexuality.
jokes.punchline: 'Didn't shove it down anybody's throat' — the unintended double entendre in a sentence about gay sex is a classic roast move, but the setup with 'he was gay, he was proud' is specific enough to sell it.
jokes.explanation: The unintended double entendre construction is a roast standard, but 'didn't shove it down anybody's throat' as the specific phrase choice is committed enough to earn a good reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The key lime pie is delicious.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: This is the worst fucking night of my life.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: And that was chocolate cake.

jokes.text: You know, Rip Taylor didn't have to throw so much confetti right on me. I don't think he did it on purpose. Most of it hit you when he tripped over the microphone cord.
jokes.setup: Carl Reiner acknowledges Rip Taylor's confetti throwing.
jokes.punchline: The image of Rip Taylor tripping over a microphone cord and accidentally showering Carl Reiner with confetti is a perfect piece of physical comedy described through understatement.
jokes.explanation: A visual gag inferred from Carl Reiner's commentary. The image of Rip Taylor tripping is funny but requires knowledge of Rip Taylor's act. Insider comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: This is the worst fucking night of my life. And that was chocolate cake.

jokes.text: Remind me to send him some flowers at the hospital tomorrow.
jokes.setup: Rip Taylor has apparently fallen at the roast.
jokes.punchline: Carl Reiner's breezy 'remind me to send flowers at the hospital' — delivered while still performing — is the perfect tone-deaf roast comedian move: acknowledge the injury, schedule the sympathy, continue the show.
jokes.explanation: Good dark understatement. The comedic contract of roasts — where harm is processed as material — is perfectly captured in 'remind me to send flowers' as a mid-set aside.

dialogue.speaker: Jon Stewart
dialogue.line: as opposed to Larry who's just old.

jokes.text: I always wanted to be mistaken for gay, you know? Because they're always the best-looking guys. Why is that? Does a guy become gay and then become great-looking automatically? Or do great-looking guys just look in the mirror one day and go, 'Oh, Christ, I'm not wasting this on chicks!'
jokes.setup: Carl Reiner riffs on Larry being called gay.
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, Christ, I'm not wasting this on chicks!' — the internal monologue of a beautiful man choosing homosexuality as the optimal deployment of his looks. The double-beat structure (does being gay make you good-looking, OR do good-looking guys choose to be gay?) builds to the kicker.
jokes.explanation: The 'not wasting this on chicks' punchline is genuinely funny and quotable — the economic metaphor applied to sexual orientation is unexpected. The build is well-structured: two hypotheses, one punchline that commits to the second.

dialogue.speaker: Jon Stewart
dialogue.line: hey, why don't you speak up? Only the people at your table know you're an asshole.

jokes.text: He's doing his act. He's killing. / Yeah, well, he's supposed to make fun of me. What is that about?
jokes.setup: Carl Reiner is killing at the roast with material that's only tangentially about Larry.
jokes.punchline: Larry's complaint — not that Carl is doing well, but that he's supposed to be making fun of Larry specifically — reveals Larry's need to be the center of even his own roasting.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character beat. Larry's narcissism is perfectly expressed: he wants to be mocked, not ignored. 'He's supposed to make fun of me. What is that about?' is a great Larry Sanders line — only he would complain that his roast isn't focused enough on him.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I don't come to your job and knock the dick out of your ass.

jokes.text: I must be honest with you. I recently had, for the first time in my life, a rectal exam. I'd never before had anything up my ass. This is not a good exam. Have you ever had this exam? They literally put a camera... up... luckily, the camera loves me.
jokes.setup: Carl Reiner confesses to having a rectal exam.
jokes.punchline: 'Luckily, the camera loves me' — repurposing showbiz vanity language ('the camera loves me') to the context of a colonoscopy camera is a beautiful misdirection and wordplay. The pause ('up...') sells the pivot.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best individual lines. 'The camera loves me' is a cliché of Hollywood vanity, and applying it to a colonoscopy camera is both specific and unexpected. The structure is excellent: the confessional setup ('I must be honest'), the building of discomfort ('I'd never had anything up my ass'), and then the sharp left turn into showbiz language. It's the kind of joke that gets quoted because it's SO specific. Justifies 8.1.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You'll either behave yourself, or I'm gonna snap your neck like a butter bean.

jokes.text: Larry Sanders and I are lovers and have been for 11 years. / Who the fuck is that? / That's Kip Addota. / We had to get him in order to get Seinfeld. / Oh. Where's Seinfeld? / The bastard cancelled an hour ago.
jokes.setup: An unknown man at the microphone claims to be Larry's 11-year lover.
jokes.punchline: Larry doesn't even know who his 'lover' is. Then the reveal that Seinfeld cancelled recontextualizes Kip's entire presence — he was only there as a package deal, Jerry bailed, and now this stranger is publicly claiming to be Larry's lover for no reason.
jokes.explanation: Excellent multi-layered callback payoff. Larry not knowing who his '11-year lover' is, the casual explanation ('that's Kip Addota, we had to get him to get Seinfeld'), and then the immediate reveal that Seinfeld cancelled anyway — so Kip's entire presence is doubly absurd — is beautifully constructed. 'The bastard cancelled an hour ago' lands perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Carrot Top
dialogue.line: It's a plate for bulimics. See, they can eat...

jokes.text: Larry would always advise me. He'd say, 'Kip, as long as what you do does not hurt you and does not hurt me, no one has any right to judge us for it.' Like today... we put salt on our asses... and we drove out to that petting zoo.
jokes.setup: Kip quotes Larry's philosophy of mutual non-judgment.
jokes.punchline: The philosophical preamble builds expectation of something sexual, then 'we put salt on our asses and drove to a petting zoo' is the most specific and absurdly visual possible subversion — it's not what you expect, yet somehow worse.
jokes.explanation: The 'petting zoo with salt on asses' joke is genuinely inspired. The structure is excellent: high-minded philosophical framing → specific absurd detail → animal context. The comedy works because (a) it's specific enough to be visual and (b) it implies something without explaining it, which is worse. One of the episode's top five jokes. Justifies 8.2.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: everyone I love is here tonight, and, um... what an honor.

jokes.text: Why is he doing this to me? / Oh, come on. It's what they do at roasts. It just sounds worse when it's about you.
jokes.setup: Larry is distressed by Kip's absurd roast material.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'it just sounds worse when it's about you' is both obvious and perfectly true — Larry is discovering the subjective nature of cringe comedy.
jokes.explanation: A tight, functional exchange. Artie's observation is a genuine insight about roast comedy's subjective sting. The economy is good.

jokes.text: Well, then I owe Carrot Top a big apology for last year, don't I? Remember when I said he would suck a cock doing a sack race? I was such a moron. I only meant it to be funny.
jokes.setup: Artie tells Larry the roast material only sounds worse when it's about you.
jokes.punchline: Larry's immediate pivot to his own previous offense — a very specific previous roast joke about Carrot Top — combined with 'I was such a moron. I only meant it to be funny' is beautifully self-aware and oblivious simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'suck a cock doing a sack race' as a previous Larry roast joke — and his sincere regret combined with 'I only meant it to be funny' — is pure Larry Sanders: insight and obliviousness in the same breath. The image of a sack race adds a layer of absurdist physical comedy.

jokes.text: He's doing a kid's show on Saturday.
jokes.setup: Larry says he needs to send Carrot Top an apology for the sack race cock joke.
jokes.punchline: Artie's flat 'He's doing a kid's show on Saturday' — delivered as useful scheduling information — implies the image of Carrot Top performing for children the day after this has been said about him at a public roast.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. The image of Carrot Top doing children's entertainment juxtaposed against the previous conversation is darkly funny, and Artie's flat tone makes it funnier. Three words of context create a joke without comment.

jokes.text: Larry found work on a poultry farm, taking blind turkeys out to shit.
jokes.setup: Kip continues with his roast material about Larry.
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'blind turkeys' and the job description 'taking them out to shit' is maximally absurdist. The image of Larry Sanders escorting visually impaired poultry to a bathroom break is magnificently strange.
jokes.explanation: The specific pairing of 'blind turkeys' + 'taking them out to shit' achieves something rare in roast humor — it's too strange to be merely offensive and too specific to be generic. Pure absurdism deployed with economy.

jokes.text: This asshole's running long. / They're all going long.
jokes.setup: Kip is still performing extended roast material.
jokes.punchline: Larry's complaint about Kip running long when Kip was never supposed to be there at all — and Artie's exhausted 'they're all going long' — is a perfect backstage comedy beat.
jokes.explanation: Functional showbiz-backstage comedy. 'They're all going long' as Artie's entire response to a crisis is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: Even way back in those days, Larry always promoted safe sex. I remember he had me go around and tag all the sheep that kicked.
jokes.setup: Kip describes Larry's commitment to safe sex.
jokes.punchline: The pivot from 'promoted safe sex' to 'tagged the sheep that kicked' is a barnyard escalation of the petting zoo joke — Kip's material is revealed to be consistently about Larry and livestock.
jokes.explanation: A callback to the petting zoo joke that develops Kip's consistent Larry-and-animals theme. 'Sheep that kicked' as safe sex precaution is specific and dark. Running gag structure emerging.

jokes.text: OK, anyway, I've been asked to inject some class into this evening. But first, I'd like to thank the hotel for having us here. You see, this thing was sort of like a last-minute thing, and, uh, Tom Arnold's asshole was booked, so...
jokes.setup: Hank speaks from the dais, ostensibly to inject class into the evening.
jokes.punchline: The setup of 'inject some class' followed immediately by 'Tom Arnold's asshole was booked' as the reason they ended up at this venue is a perfect subversion. The Tom Arnold reference is specific 1990s-Hollywood trash comedy.
jokes.explanation: The structure is excellent: 'inject some class' → 'but first' → 'Tom Arnold's asshole was booked.' The contrast between the preamble and the punchline is maximally absurd. The Tom Arnold reference is perfectly calibrated for the mid-90s HBO insider audience. Hank's commitment to classing up an event while immediately making it classless is perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: Oh, yes, the great Carl Reiner! Thank you, Hank. Thank you, Hank. Thank you very much. That's the kind of quick wit and jest that keeps you on Larry's couch.
jokes.setup: Hank sarcastically introduces Carl Reiner.
jokes.punchline: Carl Reiner's instant comeback — 'that's the kind of quick wit that keeps you on Larry's couch' — acknowledges Hank's sideman status while mocking his wit in one line. 'On Larry's couch' is the perfect image of Hank's subordinate role.
jokes.explanation: Carl Reiner's live comeback to Hank is among the episode's best. It efficiently destroys Hank by acknowledging his entire career ('Larry's couch') as his peak achievement while delivering it as a compliment. The phrase 'quick wit and jest' repeated as mock praise makes it cut deeper. Justifies 8.

jokes.text: Our next guest is a favorite of everyone from a hundred to 300 years old. No. No, he's actually a favorite of Larry's, but no one else's. Please welcome — and let's hope he can hear this introduction — Norm Crosby!
jokes.setup: Carl Reiner introduces Norm Crosby.
jokes.punchline: The triple-beat: 'favorite of everyone from 100 to 300 years old' (implies extreme oldness) → immediate self-correction 'No, actually only Larry's favorite' → 'let's hope he can hear this introduction' (hearing loss). Three jokes in one introduction.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully efficient triple-joke introduction. The self-correction in a formal introduction is unexpected, and 'hope he can hear this' lands as a clean final beat. Strong structure.

jokes.text: I thought you said Cosby. / No. I said Crosby right from the very start. You must have misunderstood me. / What a night. Thank you very much, Carl. I gotta tell you, you are absolutely adequate.
jokes.setup: Norm Crosby takes the stage.
jokes.punchline: The Cosby/Crosby confusion — with Carl Reiner's immediate denial ('I said Crosby right from the very start') — and then Norm's opening line 'You are absolutely adequate' as his 'thank you' is a perfect running double-beat. 'Absolutely adequate' is a beautifully precise understatement-as-insult.
jokes.explanation: Two jokes in one beat. The Cosby/Crosby mix-up is sharp — pointing at the casual indifference the audience clearly shares. Carl's defensive denial makes it funnier. Then 'absolutely adequate' as an opening thank-you is a perfectly calibrated put-down — damning with the faintest possible praise. Very quotable.

jokes.text: When I first met Larry Sanders, he was screwing my cousin. / And I didn't even know that he knew Harvey.
jokes.setup: Norm Crosby describes meeting Larry for the first time.
jokes.punchline: 'He was screwing my cousin' primes a heterosexual reading — then 'I didn't even know he knew Harvey' reveals the cousin's name is Harvey, retroactively making it a gay joke and a 'I didn't know you knew each other' joke simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: Excellent two-beat misdirection. The setup is completely neutral, the reveal of 'Harvey' recontextualizes everything economically. The parenthetical 'I didn't even know he knew Harvey' delivers the punchline in the most natural possible way — as a genuine surprise rather than a constructed reveal. Economy is near-perfect: nine words. Justifies 8.2.

jokes.text: He's on that new Hollywood agent diet. You can only eat while you're being eaten.
jokes.setup: Norm notes that Larry looks great.
jokes.punchline: 'You can only eat while you're being eaten' — the simultaneous double meaning of 'eaten' (food consumption / sexual act) is a clean wordplay joke. The 'Hollywood agent diet' framing makes it industry-specific.
jokes.explanation: Clean, sharp wordplay. 'The Hollywood agent diet' is a good setup, and 'only eat while being eaten' is economically constructed to work on two levels simultaneously. The rhythm is nearly perfect.

jokes.text: He knows the similarity between eggs Benedict and oral sex. You just... never seem to be able to get 'em at home.
jokes.setup: Norm Crosby praises Larry's intelligence and esoteric knowledge.
jokes.punchline: The 'eggs Benedict and oral sex' comparison — 'you can never get them at home' — is a roast classic structure but the pairing is unexpected enough to earn it. The pause before the punchline ('You just...') sells it.
jokes.explanation: The eggs Benedict / oral sex comparison is genuinely inspired — two luxury goods both unavailable at home. The pause-and-delivery structure is well-executed. This is probably the most quotable standalone roast joke in the episode alongside the colonoscopy line.

jokes.text: Earlier this year, I did the White House Correspondents Dinner, and after the dinner, the president came up to me — we're kinda friends — and he said that he asked who I thought might be good for next year's dinner, and I said, Larry. I recommended Larry, and he said, 'Gee, I don't know.' I remember exactly what the president said. He said, 'Larry Sanders doing his act for a half an hour? I'd rather have Al Gore fuck me in the ass.'
jokes.setup: Norm Crosby name-drops his relationship with Clinton and his recommendation of Larry for the White House Correspondents Dinner.
jokes.punchline: Clinton's specific objection — 'I'd rather have Al Gore fuck me in the ass' than watch Larry — is a perfect political roast joke. The specificity of Al Gore (known to be boring) + the sexual degradation + the implication that Larry's act is worse than both.
jokes.explanation: The long, slow build (White House dinner → name-dropping friendship → recommendation → Clinton's hesitation → 'I remember exactly what he said') is all in service of the punchline, which lands harder for the wait. 'Al Gore fuck me in the ass' is perfectly cast — Al Gore's specific reputation for tedium makes this more specific than a generic insult. Strong roast craft.

jokes.text: What the fuck am I doing here? I'm an actor. We do 2 different things. Comedians jerk off. I work.
jokes.setup: Bruno Kirby takes the stage at a comedy roast.
jokes.punchline: Bruno's immediate ontological crisis about being at a roast — 'what the fuck am I doing here?' — followed by the actor-vs-comedian distinction ('comedians jerk off, I work') is both character comedy and legitimate insider observation.
jokes.explanation: Bruno's actor-comic divide speech is sharp. 'Comedians jerk off. I work.' has the economy and arrogance of a line that will be quoted. The meta-moment of an actor being lost at a comedy roast is also honest showbiz observation. Very funny.

jokes.text: Isn't he supposed to be talking about me?
jokes.setup: Bruno Kirby has spent his entire opening talking about himself rather than roasting Larry.
jokes.punchline: Larry's plaintive 'isn't he supposed to be talking about me?' is a callback to his earlier complaint about Carl Reiner — reinforcing Larry's deep need to be the center of his own event.
jokes.explanation: Good callback that deepens Larry's character. His wound — being ignored at his own roast — is funnier for the repetition. The economy is perfect.

jokes.text: And I don't owe you $250, pal. You owe me $250.
jokes.setup: Dana Carvey publicly called out Bruno's $250 debt at the roast earlier.
jokes.punchline: Bruno's public counter-claim — not denying a debt exists, but reversing who owes whom — is a perfect callback payoff. The specificity of '$250' makes it real and petty.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback structure. The fact that Bruno doesn't deny a debt — just reverses it — implies there's actually a genuine dispute, which is funnier than either being right. '$250 pal' with that specific amount maintains the joke's grounded specificity.

jokes.text: The key lime pie is delicious. / This is the worst fucking night of my life. / And that was chocolate cake. / Fuckers!
jokes.setup: Larry is suffering through his roast.
jokes.punchline: Artie's sunny 'the key lime pie is delicious' while Larry is miserable, then the reveal that it's actually chocolate cake (Artie got the wrong dessert despite specifically ordering key lime), and Larry's 'Fuckers!' — the callback to the key lime pie ordering from the opening scene lands as a complete comedic circle.
jokes.explanation: The episode's strongest structural joke. The callback to key lime pie from the very first scene is paid off at the lowest moment of Larry's night with the maximum irony: (1) Artie gets the wrong pie while (2) cheerfully enjoying it while (3) Larry is miserable. The three-beat escalation — 'delicious' → 'worst fucking night of my life' → 'that was chocolate cake' → 'Fuckers!' — is near-perfect sitcom construction. 'Fuckers!' is a great button. Rewatch bonus is high — you notice the setup in scene one. Justifies 8.6.

jokes.text: I have to say, it is an honor to be here with Carl Reiner, a legend who can look back on a lifetime of bringing people laughter, as opposed to Larry who's just old.
jokes.setup: Jon Stewart pays tribute to Carl Reiner.
jokes.punchline: The legitimate tribute to Reiner pivots to 'as opposed to Larry who's just old' — cutting the honoree with the most minimal possible insult at the most deflating possible moment.
jokes.explanation: Clean roast structure. The contrast between Reiner's 'lifetime of bringing laughter' and Larry being 'just old' is efficient. The minimalism of 'just old' makes it funnier than an elaborate insult would.

jokes.text: But they say that Larry is self-centered. And I don't think so, honestly, 'cause if Larry could blow himself, well... he wouldn't need Hank, I guess.
jokes.setup: Jon Stewart defends Larry against accusations of self-centeredness.
jokes.punchline: The defense of Larry pivots into the implication that Hank performs oral sex on Larry — which is both a roast insult and a characterization of their entire professional relationship. '...he wouldn't need Hank, I guess' as the trailing punchline is perfectly placed.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest roast jokes. The character integration is exceptional — 'he wouldn't need Hank' is both a sex joke and a devastatingly accurate metaphor for Hank's entire servile function on Larry's show. The 'I guess' trailing qualifier is perfect deflation. Artie's heckle calling Hank Larry's 'personal fuck-bitch' earlier makes this a de facto callback. Justifies 8.2.

jokes.text: Hey, why don't you speak up? Only the people at your table know you're an asshole.
jokes.setup: Someone apparently heckles from the audience. Hank deploys his learned comeback.
jokes.punchline: Hank successfully uses one of Phil's scripted comebacks — the one he got right in rehearsal — at the real event. The comedy is in knowing it's scripted and watching him execute it.
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff. The joke is funnier for knowing the source — this is Hank's entire heckle arsenal deployed in one shot. The line itself is actually decent, which is also funny.

jokes.text: Oh, my... Hank, is that a heckler's retort? / Leave me alone. / I don't come to your job and knock the dick out of your ass.
jokes.setup: Jon Stewart identifies Hank's scripted comeback, then Hank deploys his second prepared line — incorrectly.
jokes.punchline: Hank repeats 'I don't come to your job and knock the dick out of your ass' — but in his original rehearsal he mangled the line ('mouth,' not 'ass'). His use of 'ass' here suggests either he's still getting it wrong or has adapted it. Either way, Jon Stewart calling it out as a retort is a perfect meta-commentary.
jokes.explanation: Multi-layered callback. Jon Stewart identifying Hank's retort as scripted is a meta-roast moment. Hank's version of the line ('knock the dick out of your ass' vs. the original 'mouth') may still be a mangled version, which adds another layer. The crowd at the roast and the audience at home both get the joke.

jokes.text: Hank, are you on something? / A little bit.
jokes.setup: Hank has been behaving strangely at the roast.
jokes.punchline: The 'Are you on something? / A little bit.' exchange is now deployed for the third time — but this time it's at the live roast, in public, with Jon Stewart asking and Hank confirming to an audience.
jokes.explanation: The running gag reaches its climax — now Hank admits his drug use publicly, to Jon Stewart, at the roast itself. The repetition has built to this: what was a private aside is now a public revelation. Perfect escalation of the gag.

jokes.text: Hank, are you on something? / A little bit.
jokes.setup: Hank has now mangled two heckler lines and Jon Stewart asks if he's on drugs.
jokes.punchline: 'A little bit.' — the same answer Hank gave Phil in the practice session, now delivered to a different person in a public context. The running gag lands perfectly as the third instance.
jokes.explanation: The running gag pays off perfectly. Three instances: (1) Phil asks during training — establishes the joke, (2) Larry will presumably be told later, (3) Jon Stewart from the stage gets the same casual admission during a live roast. 'A little bit' at maximum economy (three words) has accumulated meaning from its previous uses. The fact that Hank says it publicly, to a performer mid-set, with complete nonchalance, is what makes the third instance the strongest. Earns 8.0: the running gag mechanics are well-engineered, the character integration is high, and three words does everything.

jokes.text: Look at this. Hank's gonna ruin Larry's night. / It'll all turn out fine once Larry sees who the surprise guest is. / Is he backstage? Yes. / I'm wetting myself.
jokes.setup: Hank is derailing the roast.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'I'm wetting myself' — delivered presumably with complete composure about the surprise guest — is a perfect Artie expression of genuine excitement in the most undignified terms.
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'I'm wetting myself' is a funny character beat — a man of Artie's dignified restraint expressing excitement in bathroom terms. The surprise guest tease also builds effective anticipation.

jokes.text: And I dare say if he called me again... / Hank, we gotta bump ya, buddy. Oh, why? / Well, it's going way over, you know? I'm sorry, sweetie. That's the way it is.
jokes.setup: Carl Reiner is mid-sentence praising Larry when Artie interrupts to tell Hank he's being bumped.
jokes.punchline: The mundane mechanics of live show-bumping ('it's going way over') happening during a moving tribute, and Artie's 'sweetie' to the fuming Hank, is a perfect backstage/onstage collision.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat — the indignity of being bumped mid-event, and Artie's 'sweetie' as condescending gentleness toward a 50-year-old man, is character-specific comedy.

jokes.text: No way. No way. I had to sit through their bullshit. / Keep your voice down, will ya? / No, I won't. I mean, you can bump me from the show, but you can't shut me up. / Aw, man. / Fuck... fuck you, Artie. Just... just fuck you, man. / Fuck me? Fuck you. / You'd better calm down right now or I'll take you down.
jokes.setup: Hank learns he's being bumped from speaking at Larry's roast.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from backstage whisper-argument to full mutual 'fuck you' exchange to Artie's 'I'll take you down' is a classic Larry Sanders backstage meltdown — two adults behaving like children at an event meant to honor someone else.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe escalation. The bilateral 'fuck you' exchange is funny in its symmetry — Artie, who should be the adult, fully participates. 'I'll take you down' from the old man is a great image.

jokes.text: Come on, you pussy. Why don't you do it? Come on. Come on, big man. Go ahead, big man. And don't you push me. Oh, come on, come o... ooh! / Listen. Listen to me right now. You'll either behave yourself, or I'm gonna snap your neck like a butter bean.
jokes.setup: Hank goads Artie into a physical confrontation.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm gonna snap your neck like a butter bean.' The threat is maximally specific and bizarre — butter beans are soft and yielding — making 'snap your neck like a butter bean' both threatening and absurd. Rip Torn's Artie delivering this as deadly serious is perfect.
jokes.explanation: The episode's most quotable single line. 'Snap your neck like a butter bean' is the kind of specific, absurd threat that becomes instantly iconic. The specificity of 'butter bean' (not 'a twig,' not 'a pencil') creates a surreal image — butter beans are soft and yielding, making the simile both threatening and meaningless. Only Rip Torn's Artie can say this with genuine menace. This is the episode's standout quotable moment. Justifies 8.4.

jokes.text: Oh, don't hurt me. / That's... that's Hank and... Hank and Artie doing their... their mating dance.
jokes.setup: Hank and Artie's physical confrontation is visible from the stage.
jokes.punchline: Carl Reiner's improvised-seeming cover — 'that's their mating dance' — is perfect MC recovery. The term 'mating dance' for a near-fistfight is delightfully inappropriate.
jokes.explanation: Carl Reiner's quick cover for the backstage chaos is a great host-saves-the-show moment. 'Mating dance' as the chosen euphemism for a near-assault is perfectly calibrated — it acknowledges the intimacy of their relationship while making the violence funny.

jokes.text: You'll behave yourself? Yes, yes, yes. / OK. Sit down there. All right. Get down there. Go on. / As you can see, the evening is winding down. Look away, please. Avert your eyes.
jokes.setup: Artie subdues Hank; Carl Reiner addresses the audience.
jokes.punchline: 'Look away, please. Avert your eyes.' — Carl Reiner acknowledging the spectacle by asking the audience to un-see it is a perfect MC move. 'Avert your eyes' has the energy of covering something shameful.
jokes.explanation: Good button on the Artie/Hank confrontation scene. 'Avert your eyes' is a nice choice — theatrical and specific.

jokes.text: What are you lookin' at?
jokes.setup: Hank has just been physically subdued by Artie in front of the roast audience.
jokes.punchline: Hank's defiant 'What are you lookin' at?' to the audience after being visibly manhandled is a perfect character beat — his dignity utterly destroyed, he still projects aggression.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character button. The economics are excellent — four words doing maximum character work. Hank's refusal to accept humiliation, even when completely humiliated, is the defining Hank trait.

jokes.text: Ladies and gentlemen, Carrot Top! / No, have a seat. All right. No, stay seated, please. Stay seated.
jokes.setup: Carl Reiner announces the surprise guest.
jokes.punchline: Carrot Top is the 'surprise guest' that Artie was 'wetting himself' about. The comedy is entirely in the gap between Artie's genuine excitement and 'Carrot Top' as the reveal — an anti-climax that retrospectively makes Artie's excitement funnier.
jokes.explanation: The triple callback — (1) Artie's 'wetting himself' over the surprise guest, (2) Larry's earlier guilt about what he said about Carrot Top, and (3) Carrot Top being the actual surprise — is beautifully constructed. The reveal recontextualizes both previous jokes. 'Stay seated, please' from Carl Reiner is a good gag about the un-thunderous reception.

jokes.text: OK, come on, guys. I thought I had the stuff. Here we go. OK. I brought stuff. I thought you... God, I thought my hair was big. You have a huge head.
jokes.setup: Carrot Top takes the stage with his prop comedy.
jokes.punchline: Carrot Top's prop box apparently isn't fully together, and Carl Reiner's aside 'I thought my hair was big. You have a huge head' is a classic roast put-down that acknowledges Carrot Top's signature physical feature.
jokes.explanation: Functional physical comedy. Carl Reiner's hair/head comparison is a decent line but not exceptional. The disorganized prop setup is more relatable than funny.

jokes.text: Hey, this is great. It's a plate — ha ha! — it's a plate for bulimics. See, they can eat...
jokes.setup: Carrot Top pulls out another prop.
jokes.punchline: A plate designed for bulimics is a darkly conceptual prop joke — presumably with a hole in it or some mechanism. The setup is clear even without seeing the prop.
jokes.explanation: The bulimic plate joke is a standard prop comedy concept — dark but not executed with particular craft in the transcript. The laughter in the room presumably carries it. Carrot Top's prop comedy loses something in transcript form.

jokes.text: You know, it's now time to pay tribute to a man who needs no introduction — and definitely not his own TV show, but as you can see, that's too fucking late — please welcome the man of the hour, or as most women know him, the minute man — please welcome Larry Sanders.
jokes.setup: Carrot Top introduces Larry Sanders.
jokes.punchline: Two punchlines: 'definitely not his own TV show, but that's too fucking late' (the show exists and isn't great) and 'man of the hour, or as most women know him, the minute man' (premature ejaculation). The 'minute man' closer is the stronger of the two.
jokes.explanation: 'The minute man' is a clean roast punchline — the setup ('man of the hour') is a familiar phrase inverted perfectly. The 'too fucking late' line on the TV show is also a decent insider joke. Solid introduction.

jokes.text: First of all, let me start by saying that everyone I love is here tonight, and... what an honor.
jokes.setup: Larry takes the stage after a night of being publicly humiliated, watching Hank nearly assault someone, Seinfeld cancelling, getting the wrong pie, and enduring Kip Addota's livestock material.
jokes.punchline: Larry's sincere, halting 'everyone I love is here tonight' — delivered after all of the above — is the episode's closing irony. The gap between the sentiment and what we just watched is enormous. 'What an honor' as a final note of genuine emotion is either completely sincere or the most understated punchline of the episode.
jokes.explanation: The episode's emotional button. Larry's sincerity at the end of a catastrophic evening is played straight, which makes it both funny and genuinely moving — the Larry Sanders Show's signature register. 'Everyone I love is here tonight' is the kind of line that works because Garry Shandling can make you believe it while you just watched every reason not to. The understatement of 'what an honor' after Kip Addota's petting zoo story is perfect. Strong character integration — this is the most Larry Sanders moment in the episode. Justifies 8.3.

tmdb_overview: Artie works hard to make sure all of Larry's ""friends"" attend a celebrity roast in his honor while Hank tries to learn how to handle hecklers so he can be the roastmaster.
